notes.short: “Saul, Saul”: his name said twice, in earnest
notes.about: Saul falls to the ground and hears a voice call his name twice; in the next verse the speaker says He is Jesus. The doubled name is emphatic and fixes Saul's attention. It can also show earnest concern for the man who was persecuting Him.

figure.name: Epizeuxis
figure.means: an urgent, emphatic call that fixes Saul's attention

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse among the doubled names in Figures of Speech, where he says the figure draws special attention to the person and to the weight of the words. Barnes calls the address emphatic: the repeated name would fix his attention. Henry says the doubling shows Saul needed calling again and again, and the tender concern Jesus had for him.

cites.quote: Seven of these are used by God to man (four of which are in the Old Testament, and three in the New), the other three being used under other circumstances. When thus used, the figure calls special attention to the occasion or to the person, and to some solemn moment of importance in the action, or of significance in the words. ... Saul, Saul (Act 9:4).
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: A mode of address that is emphatic. The repetition of the name would fix his attention.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The doubling of it, Saul, Saul, intimates, First, The deep sleep that Saul was in; he needed to be called again and again ... Secondly, The tender concern that the blessed Jesus had for him, and for his recovery. He speaks as one in earnest

notes.short: “His rightful place”: Judas's end, gently told
notes.about: The prayer does not say outright what became of Judas. Read of him, as is most natural, the closing words speak of the traitor's end with restraint: he abandoned the apostleship “to go to his rightful place.”

figure.name: Euphemism
figure.words: to go to his rightful place
figure.means: the end that awaited the traitor, spoken of in softened and guarded words that do not name it

original.note: In Greek the words read literally his own place; the word behind “rightful” is idios, one's own.

notes.evidence: Brown (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the words a euphemistic or softened expression of the traitor's awful future, a place both destined for him and suited to him. E. H. Plumptre (Ellicott's Commentary) takes them most naturally of Judas and finds in them the reserve of one who could neither cherish hope for him nor pronounce the condemnation that belongs to God.
notes.limit: The writers differ on how much the words say: one hears in them the doom suited to the traitor, the other a reserve that leaves the sentence to God. Some take the words of the man chosen in Judas's place, going to his own place among the Twelve.

cites.quote: A euphemistic or softened expression of the awful future of the traitor, implying not only destined habitation but congenial element.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: some interpreters have referred the words to the disciple about to be chosen, “to go to his own place” in the company of the Twelve. If we connect them, as seems most natural, with Judas, we find in them the kind of reserve natural in one that could neither bring himself to cherish hope nor venture to pronounce the condemnation which belonged to the Searcher of hearts.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: “Ministry and apostleship”: one office, not two
notes.about: Two nouns joined by “and” can be read as one office: the ministry of an apostle, the very work Judas abandoned. The second word shows what kind of ministry is meant.

figure.name: Hendiadys
figure.means: one thing, the apostolic ministry: the office and work of an apostle

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Hendiadys and reads it as this apostolic ministry, with the stress on apostolic. Barnes calls the words a hendiadys, two words used for one thing, meaning the apostolic ministry. Calvin says the sense is plainer when expounded as the ministry of the apostleship, by a figure he calls hypallage.
notes.limit: One writer also says the second word is added to join the dignity of the office to its burden, and he gives the figure another name.

cites.at: Hendiadys, or Two for One: Nouns, p. 665
cites.quote: this ministry, yes-this apostolic ministry, with emphasis on the adjective “apostolic,” which is obtained by exchange for the noun.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: This is an instance of the figure of speech hendiadys, when two words are used to express one thing. It means the apostolic ministry.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Because the word ministry was base, he addeth apostleship, wherein there is greater dignity; although the sense shall be more plain if you expound it, “the ministry of the apostleship.” For the figure hypallage is common in the Scriptures.
